Per Article 36(2), extensions of the scope of notification follow the procedures in Articles 29 and 30. Under Article 29, the application must be accompanied by:

- a description of the conformity assessment activities, the conformity assessment module(s), and the types of AI systems for which the body claims competence, along with an accreditation certificate, where one exists, issued by a national accreditation body attesting that the body fulfils the requirements laid down in Article 31;
- where no accreditation certificate can be provided, all documentary evidence necessary for the verification, recognition, and regular monitoring of its compliance with the requirements laid down in Article 31; and
- any valid documents related to existing designations of the applicant body under any other Union harmonisation legislation.

Under this Regulation, all operators identified in Article 2(1) of the Regulation are to be understood as included within the reference to "economic operator" under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 [eu_ai_act:art_74#p1]. The context provided does not further specify the particular categories listed in Article 2(1).

Under Article 91, the Commission (which may act after the AI Office initiates a structured dialogue with the provider) could request the provider of the general-purpose AI model to supply the documentation drawn up under Articles 53 and 55, or any additional information necessary to assess the provider's compliance with the Regulation [eu_ai_act:art_91].

This documentation drawn up under Article 53 includes:
- Technical documentation of the model, including its training and testing process and evaluation results, containing at least the information set out in Annex XI, for provision upon request to the AI Office and national competent authorities [eu_ai_act:art_53#p1].
- Information and documentation for downstream providers integrating the model, containing at least the elements set out in Annex XII, such as a general description of the model (intended tasks, acceptable use policies, release date, distribution methods, interactions with other hardware/software, relevant software versions, architecture and parameter count, input/output modality and format, licence) and a description of the model's development elements (technical means for integration, input/output modality and format with maximum size, and information on training/testing/validation data including type, provenance, and curation methodologies) [eu_ai_act:anx_XII].
- A publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training the model [eu_ai_act:art_53#p1].

Under Article 83(1)(a), affixing a digital CE marking that cannot be accessed via the interface from which the system is accessed, contrary to Article 48(2), constitutes formal non-compliance since it violates Article 48. The market surveillance authority must require the relevant provider to put an end to the non-compliance within a period it may prescribe. If the non-compliance persists, the authority must take appropriate and proportionate measures to restrict or prohibit the high-risk AI system being made available on the market, or ensure it is recalled or withdrawn from the market without delay (Article 83(2)).

The list of criminal offences in Annex II includes:

- Terrorism
- Trafficking in human beings
- Sexual exploitation of children, and child pornography
- Illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances
- Illicit trafficking in weapons, munitions or explosives
- Murder, grievous bodily injury
- Illicit trade in human organs or tissue
- Illicit trafficking in nuclear or radioactive materials
- Kidnapping, illegal restraint or hostage-taking
- Crimes within the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court
- Unlawful seizure of aircraft or ships
- Rape
- Environmental crime
- Organised or armed robbery
- Sabotage
- Participation in a criminal organisation involved in one or more of the offences listed above

Per Article 37(2), the notifying authority must provide the Commission, on request, with all relevant information relating to the notification or the maintenance of the competence of the notified body concerned.
Under Article 61(2), informed consent must be dated and documented, and a copy shall be given to the subjects of testing or their legal representative.
High-impact capabilities means capabilities that match or exceed the capabilities recorded in the most advanced general-purpose AI models.

Supervision depends on who provides the model and system:

- If the AI system is based on a general-purpose AI model, and the model and system are developed/provided by the **same provider**, the **AI Office** supervises, holding the powers of a market surveillance authority under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 for this purpose.
- In **all other cases**, **national market surveillance authorities** remain responsible for supervision of AI systems.
- For general-purpose AI systems that can be used directly by deployers for at least one high-risk purpose, market surveillance authorities must **cooperate with the AI Office** to carry out compliance evaluations and inform the Board and other market surveillance authorities.
- If a market surveillance authority cannot conclude an investigation due to inability to access information about the underlying general-purpose AI model, it may request the AI Office's assistance, and the AI Office must supply relevant information within 30 days.

Under Article 23(3), importers must indicate their name, registered trade name or registered trade mark, and the address at which they can be contacted on the high-risk AI system and on its packaging or its accompanying documentation, where applicable.

Before putting into service or using a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III (except systems in point 2 of Annex III), a public authority deployer (or someone acting on its behalf) must register itself, select the system, and register its use in the EU database referred to in Article 71 (Article 49(3)).

Additionally, where applicable, such a deployer—if it is a body governed by public law (excluding deployers of point 2 Annex III systems)—must, prior to deployment, carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment covering: a description of its processes for using the system in line with its intended purpose; the period and frequency of intended use; the categories of persons likely to be affected; the specific risks of harm to those persons, taking into account information provided by the provider; a description of human oversight measures; and the measures to be taken if those risks materialize, including internal governance arrangements and complaint mechanisms (Article 27(1)). After performing this assessment, the deployer must notify the market surveillance authority of its results, submitting the required template (Article 27(3), Recital 96).

Under Article 74(12), providers must grant market surveillance authorities full access to the documentation as well as the training, validation and testing data sets used for the development of high-risk AI systems, including, where appropriate and subject to security safeguards, through application programming interfaces (API) or other relevant technical means and tools enabling remote access.

Additionally, under Article 74(13), market surveillance authorities shall be granted access to the source code of the high-risk AI system upon a reasoned request, but only when (a) access to the source code is necessary to assess conformity with the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2, and (b) testing or auditing procedures and verifications based on the data and documentation provided by the provider have been exhausted or proved insufficient.
For SMEs, including start-ups, each fine is capped at whichever is lower of the percentage or the amount specified in paragraphs 3, 4, and 5 of Article 99 (eu_ai_act:art_99#p2).
Privacy and cybersecurity risk management considerations and approaches are applicable in the design, development, deployment, evaluation, and use of AI systems.

Organizations must manage AI risks and benefits arising from third-party entities (MANAGE 3) by regularly monitoring AI risks and benefits from third-party resources and applying and documenting risk controls (MANAGE 3.1). This includes having policies and procedures in place to address AI risks and benefits from third-party software, data, and other supply chain issues (GOVERN 6), including risks of infringement of a third party's intellectual property or other rights (GOVERN 6.1). Organizations should also map risks and benefits for all AI system components, including third-party software and data (MAP 4), and identify and document internal risk controls for third-party AI technologies (MAP 4.2).

Suggested actions include: addressing legal requirements; applying organizational risk tolerance to third-party AI systems; applying and documenting risk management plans for third-party AI technology, personnel, or resources; identifying and maintaining documentation for third-party AI systems and components; establishing testing, evaluation, validation, and verification processes that address transparency without exposing proprietary algorithms; identifying beneficial use and risk indicators (e.g., inconsistent release schedules, sparse documentation, incomplete change management); enabling third parties to report known and potential vulnerabilities, risks, or biases; verifying contingency processes for mission-critical third-party systems; monitoring third-party systems for negative impacts on trustworthiness; and decommissioning third-party systems that exceed risk tolerances.

Transparency answers the question of "what happened" in the system, explainability answers "how" a decision was made in the system, and interpretability answers "why" a decision was made by the system and its meaning or context to the user.
Organizational practices are in place to enable AI testing, identification of incidents, and information sharing (GOVERN 4.3).
The physical synthesis, development, production, and use of chemical or biological agents will continue to require both applicable expertise and supporting materials and infrastructure.
According to NIST AI 600-1 (sec 2.4), the use of personal data for GAI training raises risks to transparency, individual participation (including consent), and purpose specification.

The parent subcategory is MEASURE 2.2, which requires that evaluations involving human subjects meet applicable requirements—including human subject protection—and are representative of the relevant population.

The action GV-3.2-004 falls under **GOVERN 5.1**, which requires: "Organizational policies and practices are in place to collect, consider, prioritize, and integrate feedback from those external to the team that developed or deployed the AI system regarding the potential individual and societal impacts related to AI risks."
